title: The Slave Who Invented Brazil's Vaccination
event_summary: In 1804, seven enslaved children were used as living carriers of the cowpox vaccine on the Portuguese ship bringing Edward Jenner's technique from Lisbon to Brazil. But it was an enslaved healer and barber-surgeon in Maranhão known only as 'Pai Caetano' who actually administered the arm-to-arm vaccinations across the province's interior, training local practitioners and adapting techniques for tropical conditions. His campaign vaccinated thousands of enslaved and free people across northern Brazil before any official Portuguese medical mission reached the region.
why_forgotten: Colonial Portuguese authorities credited European physicians and the crown's benevolence for the vaccination campaign, erasing enslaved practitioners from official records. Brazil's post-independence medical establishment built its founding myths around European-trained doctors. Pai Caetano appears only in scattered parish and plantation records that few historians have systematically examined.
why_it_matters: His campaign established the infrastructure for public vaccination in Brazil's vast interior, a model of community-based inoculation that persisted for generations and influenced Brazil's later reputation as a global leader in mass vaccination programs. It also reveals how enslaved African healers—drawing on their own traditions of variolation—were essential architects of New World public health, a lineage still unacknowledged in modern epidemiology.
